questions.text:
Te Haerenga ki te marae — te wāhanga tuatahi / A trip to the marae — part one

Read the text about Reitu and her class going to a marae. The passage describes how Matua Mike, their teacher, organised a marae trip but faced a problem finding a kaikaranga (woman caller) because most students are boys/male. According to tikanga, girls are not allowed to do the karanga yet as they haven't had children. Matua Mike eventually convinces his partner to be their kaikaranga.

Kuputaka: e ai ki = according to; nāwai rā = after a time; patipati = to coax/sweet talk

Whakamāramatia mai te raru a te roopū me te rautaki hei whakaea.
Explain the group's issue and how it was resolved.
questions.markingGuide:
Achieved (Paetae 3-4): Identifies that they have no wahine to do the karanga for the marae trip. States that Matua Mike's partner will do the karanga. May include that most people on the trip are boys/male. May include basic errors in details or interpretation.

Merit (Kaiaka 5-6): Explains that they don't have a kaikaranga because the girls who are going aren't allowed to karanga (due to tikanga — they haven't had children). Notes that Matua Mike is male so he can't do it. Explains that Matua Mike sweet talked (patipati) his partner into doing the karanga. Links examples with simple justifications to form a basic argument.

Excellence (Kairangi 7-8): Provides a detailed explanation covering three reasons they don't have a kaikaranga: (1) the only female people going are a few students who, due to their iwi practices/kawa/tikanga, can't karanga yet as they haven't had any children; (2) their reo teacher (Matua Mike) is male and therefore also unable to karanga; (3) the other staff going are either male or unable to karanga, because in the end Matua Mike had to convince his partner to be their kaikaranga. Provides a persuasive, well-justified argument with examples that convinces the reader and shows comprehensive understanding of the finer details of the text.

questions.text:
Te Haerenga ki te marae — te wāhanga tuarua / A trip to the marae — part two

The passage describes Reitu's experience at the marae after the pōwhiri. She goes to eat but is devastated (kua taka-ā-roto) by the food — mostly seafood and meat, which she finds slimy (hāwareware) and disgusting. She tries some kina anyway to be respectful but still thinks it's gross. She is upset (pāmamae) and vows never (korekore rawa) to eat kina again.

Kuputaka: kua taka-ā-roto = my heart sank; hāwareware = slimy; rata = to like/warm to; pāmamae = upset/feel sad; korekore rawa = never

Whakamāramatia mai ngā whakaaro, me ngā kare ā-roto o Reitu ki te kai.
Explain Reitu's thoughts and feelings about the food.
questions.markingGuide:
Achieved (Paetae 3-4): Identifies that Reitu wanted to cry / was devastated. Notes she doesn't like seafood or doesn't eat meat.

Merit (Kaiaka 5-6): Explains that Reitu wanted to cry because the majority of the food was either seafood or meat and she really hates seafood. Notes she thinks it's slimy and tastes disgusting. Explains she tries some kina anyway (to be respectful) and still thinks it's gross.

Excellence (Kairangi 7-8): Provides a comprehensive response: Reitu wanted to cry because the majority of the food was either seafood or meat and she really hates seafood. She dislikes seafood because she thinks it's slimy and tastes disgusting, but she feels like she should try some anyway because she thinks the cooks will be upset if she turns her nose up at it. However, after trying some kina she is still not impressed — it was salty and she doesn't want to ever eat it again. Shows thorough understanding of the finer details and Reitu's emotional journey.

questions.text:
Te Haerenga ki te marae — te wāhanga tuatoru / A trip to the marae — part three

The passage describes the positive experience at the marae. They enjoyed listening to kōrero o neherā (stories of old), eating delicious food, and being together. When it was time to leave, the parents helped load bags onto the bus. The boys threw the bags into the bus while Reitu helped move some down, which helped the bus driver. They all worked together to get the bags on as they were running late.

Kuputaka: kōrero o neherā = stories of old; toenga = remainder; rourou = food basket

Whakamāramatia te hāngaitanga o te whakataukī nei, "Nāu te rourou, nāku te rourou, ka ora ai te iwi" ki roto i te tuhinga.
Explain how the whakataukī "Nāu te rourou, nāku te rourou, ka ora ai te iwi" applies to the text.
questions.markingGuide:
Achieved (Paetae 3-4): Identifies a basic connection, e.g. she moved some of the bags, OR the boys threw the bags into the bus, OR the whakataukī is about helping each other.

Merit (Kaiaka 5-6): Explains that the whakataukī is about helping. She moved some of the bags down to the bus, which helped the bus driver. They all worked together to help the bus driver to get bags on as they were late, so this made things go faster.

Excellence (Kairangi 7-8): Provides a thorough explanation: The whakataukī "Nāu te rourou, nāku te rourou, ka ora ai te iwi" (with your food basket and my food basket, the iwi will thrive) is about helping people and working together. In the context of the text, Reitu moved some of the bags down to the bus, which helped the bus driver. While she was doing that, the boys threw the bags into the bus. Therefore, they were all working together and would get back to school where their parents were waiting for them. By working together, they would also get back to school in time for rugby practice. Shows understanding of the meaning and purpose of the text and links whakataukī to specific examples.
